planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Anne Bidwell blooms up to two weeks later than most summersweet selections, extending the fragrant bloom season into late summer.

directions: Site in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, watering deeply during dry spells since this selection does not tolerate prolonged drought. Anne Bidwell is a Massachusetts-origin seedling selection of the native summersweet prized for its exceptionally large, branched flower spikes, often 8 to 10 inches long, that dwarf those of most other cultivars. The abundant white, intensely fragrant flowers open in mid- to late summer, noticeably later than sister selections, stretching the pollinator season for bees and butterflies. Clean dark green foliage turns yellow in fall before drop. A strong choice for heavy shade at a woodland edge or foundation planting where a long-blooming, richly scented shrub is wanted, zone 4-9.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ripple Effect produces successive flushes of flower racemes over several weeks rather than a single bloom period.

directions: Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, keeping the root zone consistently damp for best flowering. Ripple Effect is a compact Proven Winners selection of the native summersweet notable for its habit of sending up multiple, successively opening flower spires rather than blooming all at once, which extends the sweetly scented display across much of the summer. Dense spikes of white flowers draw heavy bee and butterfly traffic against dark green foliage that shifts to gold and burgundy tones in fall. Its tidy, compact form fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without the size of older summersweet cultivars, and it tolerates heavy, wet, or clay soils better than many shrubs. A reliable, long-blooming choice for a shaded pollinator garden, zone 4-9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; named for its origin at the Fern Valley native plant collection of the Smithsonian's National Arboretum.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Fern Valley Pink is a selection of native summersweet prized for its prolific, fragrant, light pink flowers borne on upright spikes up to 12 inches long at the height of summer, set against lustrous dark green foliage. The long bloom spikes attract steady traffic from butterflies and other pollinators and make an excellent cut flower. It grows into a rounded, densely branched shrub well suited to a shaded border, woodland edge, or foundation planting where its scent can be appreciated up close, zone 4-9.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Cottondale was discovered growing wild in the Florida panhandle and introduced into cultivation by Woodlanders nursery.

directions: Grow in moist to average, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; once established it tolerates more heat and drier soil than the more common Clethra alnifolia. Cottondale is a Gulf Coast selection of the woolly summersweet, Clethra tomentosa, distinguished by very large, showy flower racemes up to 16 inches long and downy, grey-green foliage that sets it apart from other summersweets. The abundant white, spicy-fragrant flowers open in late summer and are heavily visited by bees and butterflies, and the shrub spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose colony over time. A striking, underused choice for naturalizing at a woodland edge or in a native pollinator border across the Gulf South, zone 6-9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
